VIDEO.title: You're Not Struggling With Sin — You're Thinking About It Wrong
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 6:3-14 · Episode 10 (#10 of 28 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Romans 6:3-14. All who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death, buried with Him, so that as Christ was raised we too might walk in newness of life (6:3-5). Our old man was crucified with Him so that we would no longer be slaves to sin, 'for he who has died has been justified from sin' (6:6-7). Christ, raised, will never die again (6:8-10). So consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God; do not let sin reign; present your members as instruments of righteousness; 'for sin shall not be master over you, for you are not under law but under grace' (6:11-14).

Recap with fresh eyes: in chapter 5 Paul spoke of reigns (5:14, 17, 21), and only kings reign. So there are two kingdoms: the dominion of sin and death and the dominion of grace. Adam, made to 'have dominion' (Genesis 1:26, 28), placed humanity under sin's reign; the risen Messiah brings people into His realm. Baptism marks the transfer.

Romans 6:3-14 answers the 'silly question' of 6:1-2. Grace is not freedom to sin but freedom for new responsibilities under a new dominion. Death appears in almost every verse, about fifteen times. In the Jewish mindset, covenantal authority binds only the living (7:1-4): one who has died is released from the former jurisdiction.

Three covenant categories dominate: union with a representative, transfer of allegiance, and entrance into a new way of life. Ritual washing in the Old Testament marked priestly consecration (Exodus 29:4; 30:17-21) and covenant preparation at Sinai (Exodus 19:10-11, 22; 24:3), and Ezekiel 36:25 promises clean water and a new heart. God's people are 'a kingdom of priests' (Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9).

Covenant identity is now located in Christ, not because Torah failed but because the Messiah fulfilled what it aimed at. The Roman church's clash between Jewish-background and Gentile-background believers is 'ultimately unimportant': they belong to the same King. The teacher sees a chiastic shape in 6:1-14 with 6:7 at its center.

The lesson: 'The key to overcoming sin is not trying harder, but thinking rightly. It's about faithfully reckoning that sin's reign has ended and Christ's has begun.' Not willpower, stricter rules or shaming, but reckoning what is already true (6:11). A mentor taught him that victory comes from intimacy with God; and after being wrongly handcuffed at 19, his wrists felt cuffed long after release. Sin's cuffs are off.
QUOTES: The key to overcoming sin is not trying harder, but thinking rightly.
It's about faithfully reckoning that sin's reign has ended and Christ's has begun.
The cuffs of sin have already been removed, ladies and gentlemen, and we are now free to be instruments of God's righteousness.
Every counseling issue as a pastor is ultimately a discipleship opportunity.

method.p: Read Romans 6:1-14 and mark every 'death,' 'dead,' 'died' or 'die.' (The LSB has fifteen.) Then mark every 'reign' and 'master.' Ask: whose death, and whose rule?

src.text: Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

lines.text: How is the transfer from Adam's realm into Christ's marked? By baptism into Christ. The answer to 'How shall we who died to sin still live in it?' (Romans 6:2) is union with Christ in His death and resurrection.
Study note (added): 'having been buried with Him in baptism, in which you were also raised up with Him through faith' (Colossians 2:12).

src.text: For if we have become united with Him in the likeness of His death, certainly we shall also be in the likeness of His resurrection, knowing this, that our old man was crucified with Him, in order that our body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be slaves to sin; for he who has died has been justified from sin.

lines.text: The teacher sees a concentric shape in 6:1-14 with 6:7 at the center: the Christian has been set free from sin. If the church sat with this, it would become both unified and sanctified.
Death appears in almost every verse, about fifteen times. Paul is building on Old Testament covenant logic.

For the married woman has been bound by law to her husband while he is living, but if her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning the husband.

lines.text: Priestly consecration moved a person from common life into God's holy service without dying: washed, clothed and anointed, then confirmed by sacrifices. It required God's preparation and authorization, not human initiative.
God meant all His people to be priests: 'you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6), which Peter applies to believers in Jesus (1 Peter 2:9).

left.text: Yahweh also said to Moses, “Go to the people and set them apart as holy today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments; and let them be ready for the third day, for on the third day Yahweh will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.

lines.text: Ritual washing also marked covenant renewal. The people wash, the priests set themselves apart (Exodus 19:22), God gives His law, and the people respond with their covenant vow. The washing preceded the covenant encounter with God.

left.text: Then I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean; I will cleanse you from all your uncleanness and from all your idols.

right.text: Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

lines.text: Ezekiel's new covenant follows the Sinai pattern: washing, then a new heart and Spirit to walk in God's statutes. God sprinkles water as a priest sprinkled the altar. New identity, new obedience, renewed allegiance.

Covenant allegiance is no longer oriented around the Mosaic law as covenant lord but around Jesus Christ, who fulfills the Law. Not because Torah failed, but because the Messiah fulfilled what Torah was aiming toward.

RECKON.title: Death no longer is master over Him

src.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, is never to die again; death no longer is master over Him. For the death that He died, He died to sin once for all, but the life that He lives, He lives to God.

lines.text: Kingly language again. Christ has passed through death into a life death cannot touch. Those united with Him share His new realm.

src.text: Even so consider yourselves to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus. Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its lusts,

lines.text: The formula starts in verse 11: consider, then do not let sin reign (12), then do not present your members to sin (13). 'Hey Paul, how do I do that?' Verse 11.
This is not self-effort to become more spiritual but a perception shift: rest in God's promises, abide in Christ, reckon them true.

src.text: and do not go on presenting your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. For sin shall not be master over you, for you are not under law but under grace.

lines.text: 'Under grace' because grace reigns and has dominion in the new kingdom through Jesus Christ. Verse 14 is the paradigm shift that corrects the questioner of 6:1.
Study note (added): 'so that having died to sin, we might live to righteousness' (1 Peter 2:24).

TERMS.def: Immersed into union with Christ, sharing His death and resurrection (Romans 6:3).
The self as it was in Adam, under sin's reign, crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6).
The person as ruled by sin; it is 'done away with,' made powerless (Romans 6:6).
Released from sin's claim; the LSB's rendering of 6:7 (the video reads 'set free').
To count as true what God says is true: dead to sin, alive to God (Romans 6:11).
Living in the realm where grace reigns, not under the Law as covenant lord (Romans 6:14).
Washing, clothing, anointing and sacrifice that set priests apart for God's service (Exodus 29).
A Jewish ritual immersion pool, common in the first century.

WORDS.gloss: United with, grown together. Look up: BDAG, σύμφυτος.
To make powerless, do away with.
To justify; here 'justified from sin,' released from its claim.
Instrument, tool; weapon. Look up: BDAG, ὅπλον.
To be master over, have dominion.
To wash, bathe. Look up: HALOT or BDB, רָחַץ.

BACKGROUND.p: The Law prescribed washings for priests and for cleansing from impurity (Exodus 29-30; Leviticus 15). By the first century, stepped immersion pools (mikva'ot) were common in Judea, including near the temple. The video notes the Old Testament washings were not yet mikveh immersion as Paul's readers knew it.
The Greek hopla in 6:13 can mean tools or weapons. Chrysostom took it as arms, like the same weapons in the hands of a soldier or a robber. The picture is of members enlisted under a new King.

Early Christian baptism was normally by immersion, often after instruction (Didache 7). Paul assumes his readers in Rome, whom he had never met, already share the meaning of baptism ('do you not know?').

DEBATES.h: Water baptism or Spirit baptism in 6:3?
DEBATES.p: Most read 6:3-4 as water baptism, signifying union with Christ; some read it as the Spirit's work of uniting us to Christ, which water baptism pictures. Traditions differ on what baptism effects.

The verb is dikaioō, usually 'justify.' Some translations render it 'freed,' reading it as release from sin's power; others keep 'justified,' release from sin's legal claim. The video reads 'set free.'
The video proposes 6:7 as the center of a concentric shape. Others see a simple argument from indicative (6:1-10) to imperative (6:11-14). Both readings put freedom from sin at the heart.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video reads Romans 6:7 as 'set free from sin'; the LSB reads 'has been justified from sin' (see Debates).
'About fifteen times' checks out: the LSB of 6:1-14 has death, dead, died or die fifteen times.
Genesis 1:26 and 1:28 give dominion to humankind, male and female, not to Adam alone; the video's point about representation still stands.
The captions garble one word in the pastoral story ('corn addiction'); from context it is pornography addiction, a common caption euphemism.

QUESTIONS: What does it mean to you that you were baptized into Christ's death?
How do the Old Testament washings help you understand baptism?
What 'cuffs' do you still act as if you are wearing?
How is 'reckoning' different from trying harder?
How would remembering one King change a conflict you are in with another believer?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The key to overcoming sin is not increased willpower, stricter rule keeping or deeper shaming, but faithfully reckoning what is already true: sin is no longer your master. Christians still struggle, but they must not read struggle as proof that sin still reigns. When the church lives from that shared identity, dead to sin, alive to God, under one King, superiority collapses and unity becomes possible. As a young pastor counseling young men caught in pornography addiction, the teacher felt in over his head. His mentor reminded him that every victory depends on relationship with God, so every counseling issue is a discipleship opportunity. At 19 he was arrested in Las Vegas over a ticket he had already paid; when the tight cuffs came off, his wrists felt as if they were still on. That is sin: its authority is broken, though its presence remains. For his own anxiety and pride, he reckons himself no longer cuffed.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): when temptation or anxiety comes this week, stop and say Romans 6:11 aloud, then name one way to present your members to God as instruments of righteousness in that moment.

   Once for all Romans 6:8-10: "Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, is never to die again; death no longer is master over Him.    (video) Kingly language again. Christ has passed through death into a life death cannot touch. Those united with Him share His new realm.
2. Romans 6:11-12: Consider yourselves dead to sin
   Reckoning, not willpower Romans 6:11-12: "Even so consider yourselves to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus. Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its lusts," https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+6:11-12
   (video) The formula starts in verse 11: consider, then do not let sin reign (12), then do not present your members to sin (13). 'Hey Paul, how do I do that?' Verse 11.
   (video) This is not self-effort to become more spiritual but a perception shift: rest in God's promises, abide in Christ, reckon them true.

   Under grace Romans 6:13-14: "and do not go on presenting your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. For sin shall not be master over you, for you are not under law but under grace." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+6:13-14

## Key people
- Paul: Answers 'Shall we continue in sin?' with union with Christ and a change of kingdom. [Background] He wrote to a church he had not yet visited.
- Adam: Humanity's representative, made to have dominion; his failure placed humanity under sin's reign. [Background] Romans 5:12-21, the previous episode.
- Aaron and his sons: Washed with water at their consecration (Exodus 29:4) and before every service (Exodus 30:17-21). [Background] Leviticus 8:6 records the washing being carried out.
- Moses: Told the people to wash before the Sinai covenant (Exodus 19:10-11). [Background] He read the book of the covenant and sprinkled its blood (Exodus 24:7-8).
- Ezekiel: God will sprinkle clean water and give a new heart (36:25-27). [Background] Prophesied to exiles in Babylon.
- Peter: Applies 'a kingdom of priests' to all believers (1 Peter 2:9). [Background] Also writes that Christ bore our sins so we might die to sin (1 Peter 2:24).

## Places [Background]
- Mount Sinai (named in the video): The people washed their garments and were ready for the third day (Exodus 19:10-11). Traditional site.
- Jordan River: Where John baptized and Jesus was baptized (Matthew 3).
- Rome: Believers baptized into the same King, yet divided.
- Corinth: Where Paul probably wrote Romans.

## Key terms
- Baptized into Christ: Immersed into union with Christ, sharing His death and resurrection (Romans 6:3).
- Old man: The self as it was in Adam, under sin's reign, crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6). [Background]
- Body of sin: The person as ruled by sin; it is 'done away with,' made powerless (Romans 6:6). [Background]
- Justified from sin: Released from sin's claim; the LSB's rendering of 6:7 (the video reads 'set free').
- Consider (reckon): To count as true what God says is true: dead to sin, alive to God (Romans 6:11).
- Under grace: Living in the realm where grace reigns, not under the Law as covenant lord (Romans 6:14).
- Priestly consecration: Washing, clothing, anointing and sacrifice that set priests apart for God's service (Exodus 29).
- Mikveh: A Jewish ritual immersion pool, common in the first century.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Ritual washing and the mikveh: The Law prescribed washings for priests and for cleansing from impurity (Exodus 29-30; Leviticus 15). By the first century, stepped immersion pools (mikva'ot) were common in Judea, including near the temple. The video notes the Old Testament washings were not yet mikveh immersion as Paul's readers knew it.
- Weapons or instruments?: The Greek hopla in 6:13 can mean tools or weapons. Chrysostom took it as arms, like the same weapons in the hands of a soldier or a robber. The picture is of members enlisted under a new King.
- Baptism in the early church: Early Christian baptism was normally by immersion, often after instruction (Didache 7). Paul assumes his readers in Rome, whom he had never met, already share the meaning of baptism ('do you not know?').

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "For He died Himself and was buried in the Flesh, but we have done both to sin." Homilies on Romans 10, on 6:4. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "He does not say, let not the flesh live or act, but, let not sin reign, for He came not to destroy our nature, but to set our free choice aright." Homilies on Romans 11, on 6:12. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "The body then is indifferent between vice and virtue, as also instruments (or arms) are." Homilies on Romans 11, on 6:13. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Water baptism or Spirit baptism in 6:3? Most read 6:3-4 as water baptism, signifying union with Christ; some read it as the Spirit's work of uniting us to Christ, which water baptism pictures. Traditions differ on what baptism effects.
- Justified from sin, or freed? (6:7) The verb is dikaioō, usually 'justify.' Some translations render it 'freed,' reading it as release from sin's power; others keep 'justified,' release from sin's legal claim. The video reads 'set free.'
- Is there a chiasm in 6:1-14? The video proposes 6:7 as the center of a concentric shape. Others see a simple argument from indicative (6:1-10) to imperative (6:11-14). Both readings put freedom from sin at the heart.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video reads Romans 6:7 as 'set free from sin'; the LSB reads 'has been justified from sin' (see Debates).
- 'About fifteen times' checks out: the LSB of 6:1-14 has death, dead, died or die fifteen times.
- Genesis 1:26 and 1:28 give dominion to humankind, male and female, not to Adam alone; the video's point about representation still stands.
- The captions garble one word in the pastoral story ('corn addiction'); from context it is pornography addiction, a common caption euphemism.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What does it mean to you that you were baptized into Christ's death?
2. How do the Old Testament washings help you understand baptism?
3. What 'cuffs' do you still act as if you are wearing?
4. How is 'reckoning' different from trying harder?
5. How would remembering one King change a conflict you are in with another believer?

## Application
- (video) The key to overcoming sin is not increased willpower, stricter rule keeping or deeper shaming, but faithfully reckoning what is already true: sin is no longer your master. Christians still struggle, but they must not read struggle as proof that sin still reigns. When the church lives from that shared identity, dead to sin, alive to God, under one King, superiority collapses and unity becomes possible. As a young pastor counseling young men caught in pornography addiction, the teacher felt in over his head. His mentor reminded him that every victory depends on relationship with God, so every counseling issue is a discipleship opportunity. At 19 he was arrested in Las Vegas over a ticket he had already paid; when the tight cuffs came off, his wrists felt as if they were still on. That is sin: its authority is broken, though its presence remains. For his own anxiety and pride, he reckons himself no longer cuffed.
- Study note (added): when temptation or anxiety comes this week, stop and say Romans 6:11 aloud, then name one way to present your members to God as instruments of righteousness in that moment.
